paras: The lynching of John Tibbetts took place at Perham, Otter Tail County, Minnesota, in the early morning of June 9, 1882, when men broke into the jail and hanged the boy, reported as fifteen years old, from a telegraph pole. Tibbetts was accused of murdering a surveyor and his young companion north of the town. Papers across the country carried the case, and editors later used it to discuss crime among boys and the influence of dime novels.

On Saturday, June 3, the bodies of Edward Washington, a surveyor from Bay City, Michigan, and Fred Feherbach, a local boy, were found at Red Eye, seventeen miles north of Perham. Washington had been shot, and Feherbach had been shot, his throat cut and his body struck with a club or, according to a Perham telegram, an ax. Suspicion fell on John Tibbetts, who had been seen in Perham with money and with a watch and revolver belonging to Washington.

Tibbetts fled west and was arrested at the Bismarck levee by Sheriff Butler of Otter Tail County, after arriving under the name Ford. The Bismarck Tribune reported that under Minnesota law the boy could only be sent to the reform school and wrote that if he could not be hanged he should be lynched.

Returned to Perham, Tibbetts was examined before Justice Rothpletz, and that evening a plan to lynch him was discussed openly, though nothing was done at first. About one o'clock in the morning, according to the Perham dispatch, a few men broke into the jail, forced open his cell and seized him. They carried him to the railroad track a few rods away, leaned a ladder against a telegraph pole and hoisted him by a rope thrown over one of its rounds.
Tibbetts died within a few moments while the lynchers held back the crowd with drawn revolvers, then scattered. The same dispatch said he had made a full confession the night before.

No report of arrests of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and the Perham dispatch predicted they would not suffer for the act. Within days a brother of the murdered surveyor came to Perham with a detective, and a St. Paul dispatch accused the boy's mother of urging him on and of planning to wreck a Northern Pacific train. That dispatch said public feeling strongly favored the lynching and that the mother might share her son's fate, but a Chicago dispatch called the story a hoax and said she had been declared insane six years earlier.

The white press treated Tibbetts as a 'boy murderer' and a product of sensational reading, with the Omaha Bee heading its first item 'DIME NOVELS AND BLOOD'. The St. Paul Daily Globe reported the hanging under 'MORE MOB LAW' while remarking that the mob had been orderly, and the Perham wire ran as far as Seattle. Reports of the aftermath reached Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and Memphis, and in December a Michigan year-end chronology listed the lynching under June 8.

In November the Worthington Advance, quoting the Minneapolis Tribune, wrote that the case had been commented upon by the press generally and used it to attack dime novels, lax parents and 'bratism'. None of the reports mentions the race of Tibbetts or of the lynchers, and no Black-press coverage is available for 1882.

His age was given as fifteen in the early reports from Omaha, St. Paul and Bismarck, but as sixteen in the December chronology and seventeen in the Worthington Advance. The Daily Globe placed the lynching on Thursday night, while the Perham dispatch put it at one o'clock Friday morning.

accounts.label: Perham wire
accounts.gist: A few men broke into the jail about 1 a.m., forced the cell, carried Tibbetts to the railroad track and hanged him from a ladder on a telegraph pole while holding the crowd back with revolvers.

accounts.label: St. Paul Daily Globe
accounts.gist: A mob took him from the jail Thursday night and hanged him to a telegraph pole; 'for a lynching the mob was orderly.'

accounts.label: St. Paul dispatch on the family
accounts.gist: Investigators implicated the mother and brothers, and public feeling favored the lynching and threatened the mother.

accounts.label: Chicago dispatch
accounts.gist: The story about the mother was a hoax; no such feeling existed, and she had been declared insane six years earlier.

framing.detail: The Bismarck Tribune called the prisoner 'the most brutal human fiend' and wrote that if he could not be hanged under Minnesota law he 'should surely be lynched.'
The Daily Globe headlined 'MORE MOB LAW' and 'the Boy Murderer', while remarking that the mob was orderly.
The Seattle paper printed the Perham wire under 'Lynching a Boy Murderer', noting the lynchers would probably not suffer.
The Memphis Appeal printed a dispatch reporting public sympathy with the lynching beside a denial of its story about the mother.
The Worthington Advance used the case, via the Minneapolis Tribune, in an editorial on 'youthful depravity' and dime novels.

conflicts.note: The early local and regional reports, including the Bismarck jail interview, give fifteen.
The versions agree on the night of June 8-9; the Perham wire places the hanging after midnight.
The Bismarck Tribune item combines pieces from different days and is internally inconsistent.
